JSPrismarine / @jsprismarine/prismarine

@jsprismarine/prismarine ​

@jsprismarine/prismarine is the main package of the Prismarine project containing the core (& game logic) implementation of the server.

Prerequisites ​

Before you begin, ensure you have met the following requirements:

  • You have installed the latest version of Node.js and a package manager like npm, pnpm or bun.

Installation ​

To install @jsprismarine/prismarine, use the following command:

pnpm install @jsprismarine/prismarine --save

Worlds and dimensions ​

Each worlds.<name> entry in config.json is a Level: one save with one seed, clock, set of game rules and weather, and one World per dimension. The dimensions come from a Java worldgen/world_preset named by preset, with per-dimension overrides under dimensions. A stem's generator is built by the GeneratorFactories registry, whose built-in kinds are minecraft:noise, minecraft:flat, jsprismarine:void and minecraft:debug; register a { kind, build(context) } factory to add one. Portal travel between a level's worlds is the DimensionTravel service, reached through Server.getDimensionTravel(), with the cancelable entityPortalEnter and playerChangeDimension events. The guide is docs/data-driven/dimensions.md.

JSON Schemas ​

The server uses config.json for its settings.

Draft 7 schemas for the package's JSON configuration and data files are included in the published package under schemas/. JSON object files receive a $schema URL for the build that last wrote them. Package builds and release executables use their exact version. Standalone nightly executables use the unstable npm dist-tag, which resolves to the latest unstable package. The files ops.json and banned-players.json contain arrays at the root and carry their schema URL in a leading comment. These URLs use UNPKG, so standalone server users do not need to install an npm package to access the schemas.

Block.getJavaTags() and Item.getJavaTags() expose Java datapack tag membership after the content stack loads. hasJavaTag(name) checks one membership. Their getTags() and hasTag(name) methods continue to expose Bedrock tags.

Enumerations ​

DamageCause ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/entity/DamageCause.ts:10

What hurt an entity. Carried through so a death can be reported as what it was, and so the things that ignore particular kinds of damage have something to test.

Its own file rather than a member of Entity, because DamageSource has to name both this and Entity, and Entity has to name DamageSource - which is the runtime cycle the import rules in biome.json exist to prevent. Entity re-exports it, so the older import { DamageCause } from './entity/Entity' still resolves and nothing had to be rewritten.

The name and seed are all a format reads, so a caller that has to open the save before its level exists, as WorldManager does to read the stems the save was generated with, may attach just those two.

Block ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/Block.ts:112

One block state, as the rest of the server holds one.

A data record rather than a base class: there are no subclasses any more, because the 1477 blocks and their 22079 states come out of the pack stack and their behavior out of @jsprismarine/block-behaviors's 49 families. What a block yields comes from its active minecraft:loot component, or from the mapped Java loot table when it has no component, rather than from a method an author overrode. That is why the 260 classes this replaced were able to go.

canBeReplaced() ​

canBeReplaced(): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/Block.ts:251

Whether the block gives way to a placement rather than blocking it.

The resolved state's minecraft:replaceable component or tag answers for short grass, leaf litter, water, and other blocks a placement goes into instead of on top of. The client makes the same call when it predicts a placement, so a server that answered no for leaf litter put the block above it while the client showed it in the litter's place.

The tag names Java blocks, so the state goes through @jsprismarine/mapping first: Bedrock's snow_layer is Java's snow and its deadbush is Java's dead_bush. A block built without content has no tags to read, and only air gives way.

Snow is in the tag at every depth, but Java's snow layer block overrides it: only a single layer gives way to a placed block. Not yet measured against BDS.

Returns ​

boolean

getBreakTime() ​

getBreakTime(item, _server?): number

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/Block.ts:194

How long, in seconds, the block takes to break.

Hardness on its own is not that time. Vanilla scales it by whether the tool in hand can actually harvest the block - 1.5x when it can, 5x when it cannot, which is why dirt takes 0.75s by hand and stone 7.5s - and then divides by how fast the tool mines. Those two factors are Java's destroyProgress written the other way up: speed / hardness / 30 for a correct tool and / 100 for anything else, in progress per tick.

The divisor is what Efficiency moves: the enchantment is an add_value on minecraft:mining_efficiency, which Java adds to the tool's speed.

Parameters ​
item ​

Item | null

What is in hand, or null for a bare fist.

_server? ​

isCompatibleWithTool() ​

isCompatibleWithTool(item, content?): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/Block.ts:296

Whether what is in hand harvests the block rather than destroying it for nothing.

Java's rule in one line: a block without requires_correct_tool yields to anything, including a bare fist, and one with it yields only to a tool whose minecraft:tool rules say the block is correct for drops.

A server with no content build answers yes either way. Those rules name their blocks by tag - #minecraft:mineable/pickaxe, #minecraft:incorrect_for_stone_tool - and the merged tag set only exists once a pack stack is loaded, so without one no tool could ever read as the right one and nothing needing a tool would drop at all.

Parameters ​

BlockRuntimeIds ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockRuntimeIds.ts:20

Turns a block state into the number that travels in chunk palettes.

The id is the FNV-1a hash of the block's own {name, states} compound, serialised as little endian NBT. That choice is what StartGamePacket announces with block_network_ids_are_hashes, and it is what keeps blocks modular: an id depends on nothing but the block itself, so a plugin can add blocks without renumbering anyone else's, and the server never needs a copy of the client's internal palette ordering.

The alternative the protocol allows - the id being a position in the client's canonical list - would mean shipping and maintaining that exact ordered list for every client version, and would make every plugin block shift the ids of vanilla ones.

See ​

https://gist.github.com/Alemiz112/504d0f79feac7ef57eda174b668dd345

tryGetByState() ​

static tryGetByState(name, states?): number | null

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockRuntimeIds.ts:100

The id of a block in a particular state, or null if this server has no such block or state.

The default state is enough for most callers, and getByName serves them. It is not enough for anything that builds or simulates: a roof is stairs facing four ways, a door is two halves that must agree, and flowing water is the same block at eight different depths. Those are one name with different properties, which a name alone cannot distinguish.

Memoised, because the callers are world generation and block physics - both of which resolve the same handful of states thousands of times - and building the state object is most of the cost of asking.

Parameters ​
name ​

string

The block's namespace id.

states? ​

Readonly<Record<string, BlockStateValue>>

Properties to set; the rest take defaults.

Returns ​

number | null

The runtime id, or null rather than a throw: a caller that cannot find a block should lose that detail, not take world generation or the tick down with it.

BlockState ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockState.ts:22

A block, and the exact values of every property it carries.

minecraft:oak_log is not one block but three: one per pillar_axis. Treating the name alone as the identity is what made every oriented block render wrong, because all three collapsed onto whichever was registered last.

Instances are immutable: with returns a new state rather than mutating, so a state held in a chunk palette or handed to a plugin cannot be changed underneath its owner.

toNBT() ​

toNBT(types): NBTTagCompound

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockState.ts:75

The {name, states} compound the runtime id is hashed from.

Two things here are load bearing rather than stylistic:

  • Properties are written in alphabetical order. The hash covers the serialised bytes, so a different order is a different id for the same block.
  • Each property keeps its vanilla NBT type. The tag type byte is part of those bytes, so writing facing_direction as a byte instead of an int yields an id the client cannot resolve.

The version field the vanilla dump carries is deliberately absent: it is not part of what gets hashed.

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockStateSchema.ts:26

Which properties a block has and which values each accepts.

This is what makes blocks modular. A runtime id is a hash of a block's own name and state, so a block is fully described by its schema alone - a plugin registering myplugin:cool_block needs to agree with nobody, and cannot shift the ids of anyone else's blocks. The vanilla catalog below is just the schemas that ship by default.

BlockStateSchemas ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/state/BlockStateSchema.ts:145

Every block schema this process knows: the shipped catalog, plus whatever was registered over it.

Reading a block is not per-server state and is deliberately not owned by one. A runtime id is the FNV-1a hash of a block's own name and state, so the id a chunk holds names one state and one state only, whichever server wrote it. A second server in the process can add names, and that cannot change what the first one's blocks mean.

BlockStateSchemas.register replacing a shipped name is the exception, and the only reason BlockStateSchemas.reset still exists. Packs are where overriding a vanilla block belongs, and the override path goes when this catalog loses its static caches; see section 10 of the plan.

Console ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/Console.ts:34

The plain line console: one command per line of input, one log record per line of output.

This is the in-process console for plain mode, where the server owns stdin and stdout itself. It never puts the terminal in raw mode, draws no prompt, and does no completion, so it works the same under a pipe, inside a container, from a panel that feeds stdin, and on a Node without a TTY. The interactive terminal UI lives in @jsprismarine/console.

Ctrl+C is not handled here. The process entry point installs the signal handlers that stop the server.

Subscribes to chat and starts reading command lines from the input.

Output needs nothing to be set up, so chat forwarding happens even when there is no usable input; the server attaches this console to the logger itself. Input is skipped when the stream is destroyed or no longer readable, which is what a host that closed stdin leaves behind. A pipe that stays open but never sends anything, as under the test runner, is harmless: readline only pauses it again on disable.

Calling this again after disable starts reading again. Calling it twice without a disable in between does nothing the second time.

Its own Generator methods fill the dimension the options name, and DataDrivenGenerator.forStem returns a Generator for any other stem that shares this instance's registries, caches and worker pool. Everything that depends on a PipelineKey and a seed is compiled once per pair and kept, plus recent terrain tiles shared by neighboring feature regions.

buildFullTile() ​

buildFullTile(cx, cz, seed, key?): Promise<GenerationRegionTransfer>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:1127

One finished chunk's merged region, packed for the thread that asked for it.

What a worker runs when the whole ladder is pooled. It climbs to full exactly as the main thread would and stops one step short of the Bedrock translation, which stays on the thread that holds the mapping tables.

The region is copied rather than moved. Moving it would leave this worker's holder with a detached chunk, and a second request for the same position - two worlds on one seed, a chunk the main thread let go of - would find nothing there. A copy is about 60 microseconds against a chunk that costs a couple of hundred milliseconds to build.

number

Chunk x.

cz ​

number

The nearest structure a search accepts, without generating anything.

This is what /locate asks. A structure's position is a function of the seed and the placement grid alone, so the answer comes from laying candidates out against the bare noise terrain: no chunk is built, nothing is written, and a search over thousands of blocks costs a few hundred layout attempts rather than thousands of chunks.

Synchronous, like Generator.surfaceAt and for the same reason: the command layer that asks is synchronous, and the work is arithmetic rather than a chunk.

stopGenerating(): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:1208

Gives up every chunk request that has not started yet, for a server that is shutting down.

A generator that answers one request at a time holds a queue, and a start region fills that queue thirty-two chunks at a time. Waiting for it to drain means a shutdown spends seconds generating terrain that the save it is about to run will not even look at. The request that is already running finishes, so no half-generated chunk is handed back; everything behind it rejects with GenerationStopped.

Optional, because a generator that answers immediately has no queue to give up.

void

The whole pipeline, in vanilla's order: grace period, then the cancellable event, then armor and its enchantments, then resistance, then absorption, and only what is left of all that comes off the health.

Takes a bare DamageCause as readily as a full DamageSource, which is what let the attacker be threaded through without touching any of the call sites - falling, drowning and starving never had one and still do not need one.

Records that this entity overlaps a portal block on the current tick.

Defined in: prismarine/src/item/Item.ts:568

How fast this mines one block, which is Java's Player.getDestroySpeed as far as a stack alone can answer it.

The minecraft:tool rules give the base - the first rule whose block set matches and that states a speed - and minecraft:mining_efficiency raises it, which is the attribute Efficiency's modifier writes. Java only adds the attribute to a speed already above one, so Efficiency does nothing for a tool that is the wrong tool for the block.

Dig Speed, Mining Fatigue, being underwater without Aqua Affinity and being off the ground are the four other terms of Java's formula, and none of them is modeled: there is no effect system and no swimming state on an entity.

networkSerialize() ​

networkSerialize(stream, stackNetId?): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/item/Item.ts:652

Writes an item stack in the form that carries a stack net id - an ItemInstance.

There are two forms on the wire, and at 2168 they no longer differ by one byte. This one, which an inventory, an equipped hand or a transaction carries, opens with a fixed two byte id and closes with an unsigned block runtime id; the other, networkSerializeWithoutStackId, uses a varint for both. Neither still stops early for air: up to 748 a zero id was the whole stack, and now every field is written whatever the id is. An inventory is mostly empty slots, so a stack that stops after the id truncates the packet almost immediately - which is exactly what the client reports as a bad packet on join, before any of the interesting packets are even reached.

Parameters ​
stream ​

BinaryStream

the stream to write to.

stackNetId? ​

number | null = null

the stack's net id, when the receiver tracks one.

Returns ​

void

networkDeserialize() ​

static networkDeserialize(stream): Item

Defined in: prismarine/src/item/Item.ts:791

Reads an item stack off the wire.

The layout is NetworkItemStackDescriptor, which @jsprismarine/protocol already describes: the id, the count, the aux value, an always present flag saying whether a stack net id follows, the block runtime id, and one length prefixed blob holding the nbt and the can-place-on / can-break lists. All of it, even for air.

The block lists are retained so a stack the client sends can be sent back with the same adventure-mode restrictions. The NBT compound and optional shield blocking tick remain unused here; the user-data structure isolates them from the following packet fields.

Reading the flag is what keeps every field after it aligned. It used to be read only when a caller asked for extra, which no caller ever did, so from that byte onwards the reader was one out: the lists it then walked had garbage lengths, ran off the end of the buffer and threw. Every InventoryTransaction died there - which is what left a survival block break with no sound, the packet never reaching its handler.

Parameters ​
stream ​

BinaryStream

Returns ​

Item

See ​

https://mojang.github.io/bedrock-protocol-docs/1.26.51/types/network-item-stack-descriptor/

update() ​

update(tick): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Level.ts:648

One server tick: the clock advances once, the weather cycle runs, and every loaded world updates against the new tick.

The weather goes before the worlds for the reason ServerLevel.tick runs advanceWeatherCycle before its tick lists: a fire scheduled this tick should be put out by rain that started this tick.

The worlds tick one after another in stem order, as MinecraftServer.tickChildren walks its levels, rather than interleaved. An entity that leaves one world for another during its update is then in exactly one world's roster at any point of the tick; a world ticked later skips an arrival that was already ticked this tick.

Parameters ​
tick ​

number

The server's tick counter, which the worlds pace their own work by.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

world() ​

world(dimensionId): Promise<World>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Level.ts:342

The world of one dimension, built and enabled on first request.

The first call for a dimension asks the factories for the stem's generator, builds the world and enables it; every later call answers the same instance once that enabling has finished. Two overlapping first calls share one build. A world whose enabling failed is forgotten, so the call after the failure builds it again rather than answering the same rejection for the life of the level. Only an eager stem's world generates its start region here; a lazy one is built from inside a server tick and leaves its first chunks to whoever arrives.

Parameters ​
dimensionId ​

string

The stem's key, minecraft:the_nether for the Nether. The vanilla stems share their dimension type's id.

Remarks ​

Inert on purpose. It assigns fields and nothing else: no session is built, no listener is registered and nothing server-wide is told this player exists. A player that is constructed and then rejected - by online-mode or by a ban - therefore leaves nothing behind, which is what the chat listener and the chunk scheduler entry used to do when both were claimed here and released only in Player.disable.

applyKnockback() ​

applyKnockback(directionX, directionZ, strength, _damping?): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/Player.ts:1187

Asks the client to shove the player, rather than shoving them.

The one entity the server cannot simply move. A player's position comes from their own client and is stored here as reported, so writing to it is overruled by the next movement packet and shows up as rubber-banding. A velocity is a request the client honors, and it runs the shove through the same physics as everything else the player does.

Not awaited: knockback is a consequence of a hit, not a step of it, and the damage pipeline has no reason to wait for a packet to be framed before taking the health off.

Parameters ​
directionX ​

number

Unit vector away from the blow, x.

directionZ ​

number

Unit vector away from the blow, z.

strength ​

number

How hard, with knockback resistance already taken off.

_damping? ​

number = 0.5

Returns ​

void

claimUpdate() ​

claimUpdate(tick): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/entity/Entity.ts:581

Claims this entity's one update of a server tick for the world asking.

The level ticks its worlds one after another, and a portal trip moves an entity from the world being ticked into one that is ticked later in the same pass. That world finds the arrival in its roster and would update it a second time. The first world claims the tick before updating; the second sees the claim and leaves the entity for the next tick.

Parameters ​
tick ​

number

The server's tick counter.

Returns ​

boolean

True the first time a world asks for a given tick, false for every later ask.

getRespawnPoint() ​

getRespawnPoint(): Promise<RespawnDestination>

Defined in: prismarine/src/Player.ts:1046

Where this player comes back after a death, given as a Bedrock Dedicated Server gives it.

Their own spawn point when they have one that still holds, in the world it was set in, which need not be the one they died in: a player who dies in the Nether with an Overworld bed comes back in the Overworld, as Java's findRespawnPositionAndUseSpawnBlock has it. Otherwise the Overworld spawn of the default level, which is Java's server.overworld(). A bed or a respawn anchor only holds a spawn while the block is still there with somewhere free to stand beside it, which is Java's rule and is what resolveRespawn decides; a point /spawnpoint set is used whatever is standing there. A spawn that stopped holding is cleared here, so the player is told once rather than on every death.

The caller compares world with the player's own and changes world first when they differ: see RespawnHandler.

Returns ​

Promise<RespawnDestination>

See ​

respawnPoint for the three positions the exchange needs.

Defined in: prismarine/src/Player.ts:609

Removes the player from the server and tells the client why.

Parameters ​
reason? ​

string = 'unknown reason'

Shown to the client.

code? ​

DisconnectReason = DisconnectReason.KICKED

The code the client shows beside the reason. Server.shutdown passes SHUTDOWN.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

Remarks ​

Torn down through the connection rather than by calling disable directly, so that the player and its session are released together and exactly once, and so the RakNet session is hung up on rather than left for the client to close.

That last part used to be left out: a kick sent the DisconnectPacket and stopped there, on the assumption the client would hang up on seeing it. A vanilla client does. Anything that does not - the bot harness, which after the login sequence has nobody subscribed to the packet, and which keeps pinging - held its slot and its place in the player count for as long as the process ran, because the pings kept the session from ever timing out.

changeWorld() ​

changeWorld(arrival): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/network/PlayerSession.ts:1550

Moves the player to another world and walks the client through the dimension change.

Server side first: the record is saved to the world being left, stamped with that world's dimension, the player leaves its roster, the old world's entities come off the client, the chunk bookkeeping is cleared, the position moves, and the player joins the new roster. Then the wire sequence Dragonfly, Geyser and Nukkit agree on: one ChangeDimension with the target's Bedrock id, StopSound for everything playing, NetworkChunkPublisherUpdate at the arrival, the server-sent PlayerAction ChangeDimensionAck, the arrival chunks, and PlayStatus PlayerSpawn. The change stays pending, and the client's PlayerAuthInput is dropped, until the client closes the screen with the id this handed out: see PlayerSession.completeDimensionChange.

A client sent ChangeDimension to the dimension it is already in never closes the screen, so a move between two worlds of the same Bedrock id detours through another dimension first.

A second arrival while a change is pending is logged at debug and dropped: the player is still ticked on the loading screen, and one who arrived inside the exit portal would otherwise be sent back once the 10 tick cooldown ran out, before the client ever closed the first screen. Custom dimension ids are sent after the level announces them in DimensionData.

Parameters ​
arrival ​

Arrival

The world, feet position and rotation the player lands at.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

clearChunks() ​

clearChunks(): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/network/PlayerSession.ts:818

Clear the currently loaded and loading chunks.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

Remarks ​

Usually used for changing dimension, world, etc.

Everything in flight goes with them. The two sets are only the bookkeeping; the queue of coordinates still to send and the chunks already produced but not yet dispatched are the actual work, and they belong to the world being left. Left in place, a dimension change sent the old world's terrain into the new one, and resolved the leftover coordinates against a world where they mean somewhere else entirely.

openBlockContainer() ​

openBlockContainer(at, identifier, contents?): Promise<OpenBlockContainer | undefined>

Defined in: prismarine/src/network/PlayerSession.ts:951

Opens the screen a block draws, with whatever the block is holding.

The one call the interaction path needs. Until this existed no block opened a container anywhere in this server: a chest, a furnace and a crafting table all did nothing when they were clicked, because openMainInventory was the only ContainerOpen ever sent.

The contents follow the open for the same reason they do there: a window whose contents never arrive is one the client has no reason to keep. Each packet uses the container name that screen assigns to its slots, so a furnace's fuel list arrives under its fuel name. A workstation stores nothing of its own, so no contents follow its open. A crafting table is followed by the player's own inventory under window 0 instead, which is what a Bedrock Dedicated Server 1.26.52 sent after a click on one. Repeated requests for the same open block return the current window without sending another open packet.

Parameters ​
at ​

Vector3

The block position, which is what ContainerOpen carries for a block.

identifier ​

string

The block standing there, which decides the screen.

contents? ​

ContainerEntry[] = []

What the block holds, one entry per slot.

Returns ​

Promise<OpenBlockContainer | undefined>

The window it was opened under, or undefined when the block opens no screen.

openMainInventory() ​

openMainInventory(): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/network/PlayerSession.ts:919

Opens the player's own inventory, as the client asked.

Under its own window id rather than under zero. Zero is the inventory the client always has open; asking it to open that one is asking for something it is already doing, and it answered by closing the window again straight away - which is as far as opening an inventory ever got, so no drag inside it was ever attempted.

The contents follow the open, because a window whose contents never arrive is one the client has no reason to keep.

queueMoveActor() ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/network/PlayerSession.ts:2258

Adds an entity's movement to this tick's batch.

Sending each one on its own is what made mobs move in fits and starts, and for two reasons. Every packet became its own compressed batch and its own RakNet frame, so thirty mobs cost thirty compressions and thirty frames a tick, per player. Worse, sendDataPacket queues behind any chunk still compressing - so while a walking player streams terrain, every mob's movement waited behind it and then arrived in a burst. Mobs froze and jumped in exactly the rhythm the chunks were arriving in.

One batch a tick fixes both: one compression, one frame, and one place in the queue for the lot of them.

Entity

void

One CommandData per command, each branch of its tree an overload, with overloads that come out the same folded into one. Only commands the player's permissions allow are sent, so the list is built per recipient and sent again when those permissions change.

One of the server's two halves of the respawn exchange.

Defined in: prismarine/src/entity/PortalContact.ts:48

One entity's running contact with a portal, as Java's PortalProcessor keeps it.

The world calls PortalContact.touch on every tick the entity's box overlaps a portal block, and the entity calls PortalContact.tick once per tick from its own update. RemoteConsole ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/console/RemoteConsole.ts:48

The server end of the remote console: the service a headless server runs when a host process owns the terminal.

It speaks the console protocol over the link it is given. Log records travel through the RemoteLogTransport the caller already handed to the logger; this class drives the rest: hello and lifecycle on the way up, status once a second while something changed, command and complete round trips, the subscribe level, and a graceful server.shutdown() when the host asks for one or disappears. Chat reaches the log here too, as the line console would have done, so a headless server still records it.

The server calls enable at the start of bootstrap, markRunning once it listens, markStopping when shutdown begins, and disable right before the process exits, so the last messages get out of the IPC channel first.

disable() ​

disable(): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/console/RemoteConsole.ts:136

Answers every command still running with ok: true, sends lifecycle stopping if it has not gone out yet, closes the log transport, and waits up to flushTimeoutMs for the link to drain, so a process.exit that follows does not discard the queued messages. Links without flush return at once.

A command whose dispatch is still pending here is one that stopped the server, such as stop: its await server.shutdown() never settles because shutdown exits the process. Answering it now is the only way the host sees a result instead of a closed link.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

RemoteLogTransport ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/console/RemoteLogTransport.ts:40

Forwards log records to the console process as log messages.

Every record the logger emits at or above the subscribed level becomes one message with a seq that increases by one, so the console can detect a gap. While the link reports a pause (send returned false) records queue up to the capacity; the oldest fall off and are counted. Once the link drains, a single log.dropped with that count goes out before the queued records resume, so the console knows where the hole is.

When the link closes under the transport, the queue is dropped and the retry stops; there is no one left to deliver to, and close then sends nothing.

Properties ​

ITEM_ENTITY_LIMIT ​

readonly static ITEM_ENTITY_LIMIT: 2048 = 2048

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:2267

The most dropped stacks one world keeps on the ground at once.

Neither edition publishes a number like this, and neither needs one. Java bounds its item entities with a 6000-tick despawn, and both editions merge stacks that land together, which this server does too in entity/other/Item.ts. What neither bounds is a burst. BlockUpdateScheduler lets one tick process 4096 positions, every one of which can destroy a block and roll its loot table, and a world that has just generated hundreds of chunks has that much work waiting in it. The reported crash was over 10,000 stacks on the ground, each one falling, comparing itself against its neighbors to merge, and going out to every player in range, every tick.

The number is this server's own judgement rather than anything Mojang publishes: well past what play produces, well short of what the per-tick merge pass can carry.

breakBlock() ​

breakBlock(position, player?): Promise<boolean>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:1841

Destroys the block at a position: takes it out of the world, tells every player, and plays the break where it stood.

Deliberately idempotent - a position already holding air is left alone and reported as false. Which packet announces a break depends on the breaking mode and the game mode. With server-authoritative block breaking, the default, survival reports a PREDICT_DESTROY_BLOCK in the tick's PlayerAuthInputPacket. With the client timing breaks, survival sends an InventoryTransaction, on its own or inside the input. Creative sends a PlayerAction in either mode, and a client is free to send more than one. Rather than guess which one to trust, every route calls this, and whichever arrives second finds the work already done. That is what keeps the break from sounding twice.

Struck, not broken. START_BLOCK_CRACKING was the only thing sent while mining, and that is the progress overlay - it draws the cracks spreading and makes no sound at all, which is why digging was silent until the block gave way.

The material comes from the runtime id, the same way a break's destroy event gets it: the client looks the block up and plays whatever that block is made of.

The sound goes to everyone near but the one striking, whose client plays its own hits in either breaking mode. A Bedrock Dedicated Server 1.26.52 sends the striker none. This one reached them too, and with their client's own hits it sounded like digging at several times the speed.

isRainingAt() ​

isRainingAt(x, y, z): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:2128

Whether rain is falling on one position, Java's Level.isRainingAt.

Three of Java's four conditions: it has to be raining, the position has to see the sky, and nothing may stand above it. The fourth is the biome's precipitation, which is a temperature curve over the height that neither edition publishes in a form this repository holds, so every biome counts as rainy here and fire in a snowy one is put out where Java would leave it burning.

The sky test is the light engine's. Full sky light means an unobstructed column: sky light loses at least one per step the moment it has to travel sideways, so 15 at a position and nowhere short of the sky above it are the same statement. The engine already keeps it per block and updates it with every write, which is the whole reason not to walk the column here - World.topOfColumn answers per chunk at sub chunk resolution, so one block on a hilltop would shelter the whole chunk from the rain.

It is also Java's own test rather than an approximation of it. Level.canSeeSky reads the MOTION_BLOCKING heightmap, which a fire does not raise because it has no collision; a fire does not dampen light here either, so the position it stands in still reads 15.

Parameters ​
x ​

number

y ​

number

z ​

number

Returns ​

boolean

False for a position in a chunk whose light the engine has not computed, which is also what a fire there would answer: nothing is ticking it. Always false in a dimension without a sky, where Java's hasSkylight is false and nothing can see rain.

loadChunk() ​

loadChunk(x, z, options?): Promise<Chunk>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:1163

Loads a chunk in a given x and z and returns its.

A request for a chunk that is already being loaded joins that one rather than starting a second. They arrive together constantly - the preload asks for a batch of thirty-two in one turn, and every player whose view distance reaches a chunk asks for it as well - and each duplicate was a whole chunk generated and then thrown away, because the last one to finish overwrote the others in the map. Worse than wasted: two callers held two different objects for one position, so a block written into one was invisible through the other.

Parameters ​

number

x coordinate.

z ​

number

z coordinate.

options? ​

ChunkRequestOptions

How badly the chunk is wanted. A caller that joins a load already in flight and wants it more than whoever started it moves that load up the generator's queue, so a chunk asked for as the far rim and then stood on does not keep the turn it was given when nobody needed it.

Returns ​

Promise<Chunk>

Throws ​

When the world has been closed, since its provider is gone and a chunk generated now would be generated after the save that was meant to persist it.

randomTickChunks() ​

randomTickChunks(): RandomTickChunk[]

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:2163

Where this tick's random draws land: Java's ServerLevel.tickChunks, in two halves.

Only a chunk a player ticket holds is simulated, so an empty server draws nothing at all however much of the world is in memory - which is also why nobody's furnaces burn while they are logged off. And within a chunk, only the sections whose palette holds something that takes random ticks, which is Java's LevelChunkSection.isRandomlyTicking; see sectionTakesRandomTicks. The three hundred blocks of air over an Overworld column and the stone under it are both skipped.

The section test has to be Java's rather than merely cheap, because the draw state is one counter shared across the world: a section drawn for that Java skips steps the counter and moves every position drawn afterwards. Public for the same reason World.loadedBlockAt is: WorldSystems is handed the world's reads rather than the world itself.

Returns ​

RandomTickChunk[]

One entry per simulated chunk, with its randomly ticking sections.

Writes this world to disk: every player in it, every changed chunk, the level data.

Queued behind whatever save is already running rather than run beside it. A caller that asks for a save gets one, so this waits its turn instead of declining like the autosave does, but it never writes at the same time as another pass.

saveChunks() ​

saveChunks(): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:2928

Saves changed chunks into disk.

In batches with a yield between them, for the same reason the preload runs in batches: writing a chunk is synchronous, so Promise.all over every changed chunk was one uninterrupted run of work. The first autosave after a start region preload has all 441 chunks to write and held the event loop for ten seconds - the server froze solid, and the tick loop came back announcing it had skipped two hundred ticks.

A failed chunk write is logged and left dirty for retry. Other chunks in the pass still save, and the next pass tries the failed chunk again.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

updateBlockCracking() ​

updateBlockCracking(mining): Promise<boolean>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:1462

One tick of mining: the particles off the face being mined, then the crack progress.

A Bedrock Dedicated Server sends this pair every tick for as long as a block is being mined. The particles leave from the block's center and carry its runtime id, which the client textures them with. The progress goes to the block's corner, like the start and the stop.

The block can change while it is mined: another player breaks it, or a command or a flood replaces it. The cracks belonged to the block that was there, so they stop with it.

Parameters ​
mining ​

BlockMining

What is being mined.

Returns ​

Promise<boolean>

False when the block is no longer the one being mined, in which case its cracks were stopped and nothing else was sent.

Lifecycle ​

disable() ​

disable(): Promise<void>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:658

On disable hook.

The order is the whole of it. Marking the world closing stops the preload asking for more chunks and stops the tick; waiting for the start region means every chunk that was generated is in this.chunks before the save walks it; and the provider is closed last, once nothing is left that could ask it for anything.

An autosave a tick started is one of those things. World.save waits for it before writing anything of its own, so by the time the level closes the provider no write is outstanding - closing the database under one is the same failure the start region race used to cause. The provider itself is the level's to close, once every world of the save has been through this.

Returns ​

Promise<void>

Service.disable

CommandExecutor ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/CommandExecutor.ts:13

Something that can issue a command and be answered.

A player and the server console have exactly this much in common: a name and somewhere to put a reply. They are not the same kind of thing otherwise - one stands at a position in a world and the other is a terminal attached to the process - so this is an interface rather than a shared base class. Making the console an entity to get these four methods is what forced isPlayer() and isConsole() to exist in the first place.

ConfigDocument ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/ConfigDocument.ts:26

A config file held as text, edited one path at a time.

Reading parses the text; writing changes only the part of the text the path names, so a comment or a blank line a person put in the file stays where it was. Replacing a value replaces everything under it, including comments inside a replaced list or map, since there is nothing to attach them to afterwards.

Left out by an adapter with no live world behind it, which sends the caller back to the drop it would have made on its own.

DataDrivenGeneratorOptions ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:115

How a DataDrivenGenerator is built.

Properties ​

biomeSource? ​

readonly optional biomeSource?: BiomeSourceDefinition

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:136

The biome layout of the default key, as the biome_source of a level stem describes it.

A definition rather than a built BiomeSource, because the worker threads build their own generator and an object with closures cannot cross a thread. A multi_noise preset resolves through the reports/biome_parameters registry. Defaults to the minecraft:overworld preset.

carve? ​

readonly optional carve?: boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:140

Whether to run the carvers. On by default.

chunks? ​

readonly optional chunks?: ChunkPoolOptions

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:199

Where to run whole chunks, and how many at a time.

Absent by default, which builds them on this thread. This is the pool that pays: a terrain pool leaves the decoration pass and the structure layout here, which is 168 of the 239 milliseconds a chunk costs, so no worker count takes it past 1.33 times. A pool of whole chunks makes all but the Bedrock translation parallel.

Pool options are alternatives, not layers. DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.stages takes precedence when supplied; otherwise this option takes precedence over DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.terrain, because a worker running the whole ladder runs its own terrain inside it.

concurrency? ​

readonly optional concurrency?: number

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:163

How many chunks of one world are built at once.

Defaults to DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY. A shutdown refuses everything past this depth straight away, so a caller that wants a shutdown to drop a particular request has to keep the depth below the number of requests it makes.

decorate? ​

readonly optional decorate?: boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:138

Whether to run the decoration pass. On by default; a terrain test turns it off.

dimension? ​

readonly optional dimension?: DimensionType

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:125

The dimension the instance's own Generator methods fill. Defaults to the Overworld.

With DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.noiseSettings and DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.biomeSource this is the default PipelineKey; DataDrivenGenerator.forStem serves any other.

noiseSettings? ​

readonly optional noiseSettings?: string

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:127

The worldgen/noise_settings identifier of the default key. Defaults to minecraft:overworld.

registries ​

readonly registries: JavaWorldgenRegistries

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:117

The Java registries, already read off disk.

stages? ​

readonly optional stages?: StagePoolOptions

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:185

Where pure terrain and features status bodies run, sharing one holder map on this thread. A worker receives the terrain tiles it reads and returns only its feature patches.

Use this when requests overlap: unlike DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.chunks, this keeps shared neighborhood work in one scheduler instead of rebuilding it in worker-local schedulers. It takes precedence over DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.chunks and DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.terrain when more than one pool option is supplied.

structureBuilders? ​

readonly optional structureBuilders?: ReadonlyMap<string, StructureBuilder>

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:148

Overrides the builder for a worldgen/structure type, which a test uses to isolate one.

structures? ​

readonly optional structures?: boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:146

Whether to place structures. On by default, and only meaningful when the decoration pass runs, because Java places a structure's pieces inside the decoration step the structure names.

templates? ​

readonly optional templates?: TemplateSource

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:155

Where the structure templates template and fossil stamp come from.

Absent by default: the templates are .nbt inside Mojang's server jar rather than in the datapack the rest of the registries are read from, so a caller that wants them says so.

terrain? ​

readonly optional terrain?: TerrainPoolOptions

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:175

Where to run the terrain bodies, and how many at a time.

Absent by default, which runs them on this thread. A pool is worth about 4.7 times one thread at five or six workers on an Apple M1 Pro, and less past that, because six of its eight cores are performance cores and a worker is a whole V8 isolate.

Only terrain goes to a worker. It writes radius 0, its own chunk and nothing else, so two of them can never touch the same block. Use DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.stages to move features as well.

DimensionType ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/DimensionType.ts:33

How tall a dimension is, where its floor sits, and what the client and the save call it.

Every vertical bound in the chunk stack derives from one of these rather than from a constant, because the three vanilla dimensions do not agree on any of them: the Overworld starts at -64 and is 384 blocks tall, the Nether starts at 0 and is 128 as far as the client is concerned, the End starts at 0 and is 256.

The sub chunk index is the y coordinate shifted right by four, and stays signed: index -4 is the Overworld's bottom sub chunk, covering y -64 to -49. That is also exactly how the index byte is stored in a Bedrock world's sub chunk records, so nothing needs rebasing on the way to disk.

EntitySpawn ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/EntitySpawn.ts:12

A mob world generation decided should exist, recorded rather than created.

The generator builds chunks and knows nothing about the world they will belong to - it has no entity list to add to, and a chunk may well be generated long before anything asks for it. So a pass that builds a village says "a villager belongs here" and the world creates it when the chunk is first loaded.

Deliberately data rather than an Entity: an entity needs a Position, a position needs a world, and a world is exactly what the generator does not have.

locate()? ​

optional locate(request): StructureSearchResult | undefined

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:193

The nearest structure a search accepts, without generating anything.

This is what /locate asks. A structure's position is a function of the seed and the placement grid alone, so the answer comes from laying candidates out against the bare noise terrain: no chunk is built, nothing is written, and a search over thousands of blocks costs a few hundred layout attempts rather than thousands of chunks.

Synchronous, like Generator.surfaceAt and for the same reason: the command layer that asks is synchronous, and the work is arithmetic rather than a chunk.

Optional, because a generator that places no structures has nothing to find.

Parameters ​
request ​

StructureSearchRequest

Where to search from, how far, and which structures count.

Returns ​

StructureSearchResult | undefined

The nearest match, or undefined when the radius held none.

raiseUrgency()? ​

optional raiseUrgency(cx, cz, urgency): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:175

Says that a chunk already asked for is wanted more than it was.

A chunk is requested once and waited on by everybody who wants it, so the band it was given is whoever asked first. A rim chunk queued as idle is the chunk a player is standing on a moment later, and nothing else would move it up.

Only affects a request still waiting for a worker. One already being built finishes at the speed it was going to finish at either way.

Optional, because a generator with no queue has no turn to move.

Parameters ​
cx ​

number

Chunk x of the request.

cz ​

number

Chunk z of the request.

urgency ​

"idle" | "immediate" | "soon"

The band to move it into. Never lowers one.

Returns ​

void

stopGenerating()? ​

optional stopGenerating(): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:256

Gives up every chunk request that has not started yet, for a server that is shutting down.

A generator that answers one request at a time holds a queue, and a start region fills that queue thirty-two chunks at a time. Waiting for it to drain means a shutdown spends seconds generating terrain that the save it is about to run will not even look at. The request that is already running finishes, so no half-generated chunk is handed back; everything behind it rejects with GenerationStopped.

Optional, because a generator that answers immediately has no queue to give up.

Returns ​

void

surfaceAt()? ​

optional surfaceAt(x, z, seed?): SurfaceProbe

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:148

The topmost block of one column, without generating the chunk it is in.

The answer comes from the bare terrain: no surface rule has run and nothing has decorated, so a flooded column reads as water and a wooded one reads as the ground under the trees rather than as a canopy. That is Java's ChunkGenerator.getBaseHeight, and it is what a spawn search wants - whether a player can stand here is a question about the land, and answering it by generating a finished chunk costs four orders of magnitude more.

Optional, because a generator with no cheaper answer than its own chunks has nothing to add here and a caller falls back to generating one.

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/JsonConfigTypes.ts:77

The world seed, read the way Java reads the text in its world creation box: a value that parses as a 64-bit integer is that integer, and anything else is its String.hashCode.

Spell it as a string. A Java seed is a 64-bit integer and a JSON or YAML number is a double, which is exact only below 2^53. Written as a number, 8475011743740320021 is read back as 8475011743740319744 and generates a different world. A number is still accepted for configs written before this, and is exact for seeds below 2^53.

Which packs to compose out of a BDS behavior_packs folder, by header UUID, or 'all' for every pack the folder holds.

Defaults to the vanilla behavior pack alone. BDS ships chemistry, the editor, the server script libraries and four experimental toggles in that folder, and a world composes those only when it turns them on; a server aiming at vanilla parity turns none of them on. Education Edition content is out of scope by plan section 12 decision 8, and the editor's five editor: entities are tools for a world author rather than content a server serves.

The packs are on disk either way, so naming one here is how a server that does want it opts in.

PipelineKey ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:353

What picks one compiled pipeline out of a generator shared between dimensions: the settings a level stem names and the dimension it fills. The seed is the other half of the cache key and travels separately, because one key serves every world on the server that uses that stem.

Plain data, because every task carries its key across the worker boundary and the worker compiles the pipeline from it. One generator and one worker pool therefore serve the Overworld, the Nether and the End instead of three of each.

ParseTargetSelector() ​

ParseTargetSelector(__namedParameters): Entity[]

Defined in: prismarine/src/utils/ParseTargetSelector.ts:31

Parse target selector argument.

Parameters ​

__namedParameters ​
entities ​

Entity[]

input ​

string

source ​

Entity

Returns ​

Entity[]

The entities matching the target query

Remarks ​

A target selector is made up of 3 parts:

  • First there's the @ (at symbol) part, notifying us that this is in fact a target selector

  • Secondly there's the target selector type (a, e, p, r, s), this specifies what kind of entities we should query for and in what way.

  • Thirdly there's the arguments, they are split up in a comma-separated list in the argument=value format.

This results in an input similar to: @e[type=player,gamemode=creative,limit=3]

asyncCommand() ​

asyncCommand(run): (context) => number

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/Command.ts:43

Wraps a command body that has work to await as a Brigadier command.

CommandDispatcher.execute is synchronous and upstream Brigadier's Command.run returns an int, so a body cannot hand the dispatcher a promise: the dispatcher would push it into its result list and give it to the ResultConsumer unresolved. Almost every command here answers the sender, touches a world or shuts the server down, so almost every body has to await something.

The body is started synchronously and its promise is parked on a queue, which collectAsyncCommands hands back to CommandManager.dispatchCommand. The command is awaited there, so nothing is fired and forgotten: a rejection still reaches the sender and the feedback string a body returns is still broadcast.

Parameters ​

run ​

(context) => Promise<CommandFeedback>

Returns ​

(context) => number

Resolves every Java identifier the loaded pack stack references and reports the ones nothing accounts for.

Non-strict is a report rather than a refusal, for the same reason the content build reports the defaults it had to invent instead of stopping: a server that would otherwise run should run, and the operator should be told exactly what will be missing. Each unaccounted identifier is one error-severity diagnostic naming the pack and the file, so the startup line that counts content errors counts these too. Strict turns the same list into UnmappedIdentifierError.

A reviewed loss is not reported. It is already written down, with a reason and a reference, in @jsprismarine/mapping's loss list, and the parity dashboard counts it from there.

contentRegistryIds() ​

contentRegistryIds(content): ContentRegistryIds

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/vanillaCommands.ts:58

The four registries whose contents a command argument validates against.

Mojang's published command enums are frozen at the version the table was generated from, so validating against them alone refuses a pack's own mypack:dragon at parse for an entity this server can spawn. These four are the registries a host verb resolves an id against and a pack can extend, so each is offered alongside Mojang's list rather than instead of it.

The registries left out fail that test for their own reasons. minecraft:damage_type has no registry on this server at all, and minecraft:mob_effect uses Mojang's published list because the host keeps no custom effect registry. minecraft:attribute, minecraft:particle_type and minecraft:worldgen/biome are not validated by anybody: Bedrock publishes no enum for them, so they already reach a command body as an unchecked string.

Parameters ​

Builds the eight block adapter members over one dimension's storage.

set commits the write before it raises onPlace, because the hook is documented to run with the new state already readable, and notifies the neighbors afterwards so a behavior that writes its own state during onPlace has done so before anything reads it back.

A write that leaves the same block standing raises onBlockStateChange instead of onPlace, once per state value that moved. That is what the two hooks are documented to mean, and it is also what makes the write terminate: a door opens by rewriting its own open_bit, so onPlace would call the family that is calling it.

createNoiseGeneratorFactory() ​

createNoiseGeneratorFactory(): GeneratorFactory

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/factories/noise.ts:48

A minecraft:noise factory whose stems share one DataDrivenGenerator.

The first stem built opens the generator from the context's registries, with a pool of worker threads sized by the context's workers or the core count. Every stem after that, the Nether's and the End's included, gets a view of the same generator keyed by its settings, its biome source and its dimension, so a server runs one pool of min(6, cores - 2) workers rather than one per dimension. The stem's settings names a worldgen/noise_settings document or carries one inline; the inline form travels under a private id. A host that cannot run workers generates on the server thread and says so once.

One factory per GeneratorFactories registry, which is one per server: the registry's stopGenerating reaches the shared generator through any of the views it built.

Returns ​

GeneratorFactory

Throws ​

When the Java data is not on disk, or the settings id is not a registered worldgen/noise_settings document, or the biome source cannot be built.

deferCommandWork() ​

deferCommandWork(work): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/Command.ts:64

Parks work a synchronous command body started, so the dispatch awaits it.

The seam @jsprismarine/commands defines is synchronous - a host verb answers how many blocks changed or whether the player exists - while nearly every server API that carries the change out is asynchronous, because the change goes out over the wire. A host verb therefore decides the answer synchronously and hands the delivery here.

It is the same queue asyncCommand uses and the same guarantee: collectAsyncCommands hands the promises to CommandManager.dispatchCommand, which awaits them before any feedback goes out, so a rejection reaches the sender rather than becoming an unhandled rejection.

work ​

Promise<CommandFeedback>

Returns ​

void

toPacketCompressionLevel() ​

toPacketCompressionLevel(raw): number

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/Config.ts:145

Clamps a configured zlib level to the range zlib accepts.

zlib takes -1 (its own default) through 9 and errors on anything else. The value comes straight out of a hand edited config file, and an unchecked 10 reached deflate as a rejection on the chunk sending path, which is nowhere near where the typo was, and used to take the server's tick down with it. Clamping keeps a bad number a bad number rather than an outage.

Parameters ​

raw ​

unknown

The value read from the config file, of whatever type the file held.

Returns ​

number

An integer from -1 to 9, or the default of 7 when raw is not an integer.

unwiredWorld() ​

unwiredWorld(options?): ServerWorldAdapter

Defined in: prismarine/src/content/world/unwired.ts:33

An adapter whose every member throws.

The four facts a dimension knows about itself without a world behind it, its identifier, its bounds and its seed, are answered rather than thrown, because a caller that only reads them is asking a question the server can honestly answer and failing it would hide the members that genuinely are missing.
